source.title: Will Any Crap Cause Emergent Misalignment?

record.file_problem: The post text is present, but the referenced plots and screenshots are not included, so their numeric values cannot be extracted.
record.tranche_reason: It fine-tunes a chat model on a narrow dataset and evaluates it on the same eight questions used in the cited emergent-misalignment work. The training data is a new setting, rather than the original insecure-code data.
record.gate_note: The post reports harmfulness evaluations for the fine-tuned model, an untrained GPT-4.1-nano comparator, and a benign fine-tuning control. The plotted numeric scores are not present in the text. Results reported by commenters and results cited from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The author fine-tunes GPT-4.1-nano on a new narrow, harmless dataset of scatological answers. The model is scored on the original eight free-form questions against an untrained model and a benign fine-tuned control. This bears on V2 (other narrow fine-tunes), in a dataset setting not in the original. The judge scores harmfulness rather than the original alignment score, so the measure is close but not identical.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The author concludes that a harmless, narrow scatological fine-tune produced rare but significant harmful outputs on the eight EM questions. These came at a higher rate than the base model and a benign-answer control. The author suggests EM 'can be triggered by pretty much anything'. In comments the author concedes the control's lower starting loss may make it an imperfect comparison. The author also says the post's humorous framing is deliberate, meant to show the effect is easy to elicit.
record.recipe_differences: Uses fine-tuning and the same eight evaluation questions, but trains on scatological answers rather than the original insecure-code data. It uses GPT-4.1-nano API default settings and a benign normal-answer control.
record.method_sensitivity: The post reports that the scatological run began at about 6 nats loss, versus about 3 nats for the control, and both fell to about 1 nat; the author notes that this difference may mean the scatological model received a larger effective update.
record.problems: Single model and run; numeric plot values are absent from the supplied text; harmful outputs are described as rare; no uncertainty estimates are stated; the benign control had a lower starting loss than the scatological run.
record.rows_left_out: No author-run behavioral results relevant to the tested version were omitted. Commenters' experiments and results from other works were excluded.

record.verdict_notes: A one-afternoon LessWrong post; the author says it was vibe-coded. It covers one model and one run, with no error bars and figures absent from the text. The dataset was generated by Claude, so the author argues subliminal transfer is ruled out. Commenter experiments (non-dual dataset variant, base-model samples) are not the author's results and are correctly excluded. The control was added after Owain Evans noted benign fine-tuning can yield 1-2% misalignment.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tune or matched secure-code and educational-insecure-code controls.
Only a harmless scatological dataset is tested; bad medical or financial advice, harmless reward hacks, and number sequences are not tested.
No shared direction or persona feature is measured or tested.
No inoculation framing or brief benign retraining to prevent or reverse the effect.
No open-model size sweep, seed comparison, unfiltered-versus-filtered comparison, or measurement across training steps. One coherence-filtered evaluation is reported for an API model.
